title: There's a Playbook for College. There Should Be One for Marriage. Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://aaronrenn.substack.com
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Renn argues that young people make critical decisions about marriage and children under a structural disadvantage: they make those decisions before they have the psychological capacity — typically not developed until the mid-30s — to emotionally connect to the future consequences of present choices. The 'end of history illusion' captures the problem: we underestimate how much we will change in the future, which means the 35-year-old who regrets not having children could not have felt the weight of that future regret when she was 25 and making the choice. Unlike career or college decisions, where real-world feedback arrives quickly when something goes wrong, the costs of forgoing marriage and children are often delayed by decades — appearing fully only in middle age or later, by which point the window to choose otherwise has often closed. Renn illustrates with the WSJ profile of Amy Kant: a successful, single, childless 65-year-old navigating heart surgery recovery by coordinating a spreadsheet of friends who have their own households, while acknowledging that a 'chosen family' has limits that biological family does not. His proposal is that young people deserve an explicit 'playbook for marriage' that front-loads the costs, makes the future legible, and creates the equivalent of the institutional guidance (financial aid counseling, career services, orientation) that exists for college decisions. The article does not argue that everyone should marry or have children, but that the decisions about whether to do so should be made with clearer awareness of their future implications — awareness that the 'end of history illusion' systematically prevents.
points: The asymmetry of feedback is Renn's sharpest structural point: career mistakes produce immediate consequences (layoffs, bad assignments, missed promotions) that allow for course correction, while the consequences of opting out of marriage and family arrive decades later when correction is much harder.

The 'end of history illusion' is well-documented in psychology: we consistently underestimate how much we will change in the future while vividly remembering how much we changed in the past — and it applies with particular force to life-stage decisions whose consequences are most visible in stages we haven't yet reached.

The Amy Kant portrait is not an argument that single, childless life is wrong, but a concrete illustration of a specific vulnerability: health crises in later life are structurally more difficult to manage without children or a spouse, and social networks built on friendship rather than family have different durability under extended demand.

Renn's mid-30s transition observation — the developmental shift that allows genuine emotional connection to one's future story arc — suggests that the problem is not individual weakness but a structural mismatch between when the decisions are made and when the capacity for evaluating them arrives.

The 'playbook' proposal is an institutional design suggestion: just as college has orientation, financial counseling, and career advising, the culture around early adulthood needs honest, non-moralistic conversation about the real long-term costs of the most consequential decisions young people make.
quotes: When I was with her and looked at her lying in that hospital bed, for the very first time in my life it hit me. When I'm old and lying in that hospital bed, who is going to come stay with me? The answer was, nobody. Nobody would be coming to stay with me. That was a sobering thought.

Younger people know how much they've changed in the past — Oh, how much I've changed! How much I've learned! How much I've grown! — but not how much they will change in the future. Nor can they really emotionally relate to the later-in-life consequences of decisions made today.

In my observation, it's not until people get to be roughly 35 years old that they gain the ability to really understand that they will change in the future, and to emotionally connect to the future story arc of their life.

Beyond that, the positive consequences of forgoing these elements of life — more freedom, more fun — arrive immediately whereas the negative ones don't show up for potentially decades. This is very unlike decisions around college or career, where real-world feedback arrives quickly if you make a mistake.

Add it up and it's a recipe for many people to only have the magnitude of what they have done fully hit them at a time at which there's only a limited runway to change course — or even when it's too late.

A longtime college friend serves as her healthcare proxy, and Kant maintains a spreadsheet of friends to coordinate visits when she's ill. Still, she understands the boundaries of a chosen family. Her friends have their own households to manage; some have already died.
The costs of putting off marriage and children don't show up for decades — and by the time they do, the window to choose otherwise has often closed.
